misconceptions.text: In stratified sampling, takes an equal number from each stratum, e.g. for a sample of 50 from three groups writes $50 \div 3 \approx 17$ from each group.
misconceptions.correction: Each stratum must be represented in proportion to its size. Use $\frac{\text{stratum size}}{\text{population size}} \times \text{sample size}$: juniors $\frac{84}{300} \times 50 = 14$, adults $26$, seniors $10$.

misconceptions.text: Rounds every stratum to the nearest whole number without checking the total, e.g. strata of $13.5$, $15.75$, $12$, $11.25$, $7.5$ become $14 + 16 + 12 + 11 + 8 = 61$ when the sample size is 60.
misconceptions.correction: After rounding, check that the strata add up to the required sample size. If they do not, adjust a stratum whose value was closest to the halfway point. Here $13.5$ and $7.5$ are both exactly halfway, so round one of them down (e.g. $13.5$ to $13$, giving $13 + 16 + 12 + 11 + 8 = 60$) so that the total is exactly 60.

misconceptions.text: Thinks an opportunity sample is random because the interviewer "didn't pick anyone on purpose", e.g. "I asked whoever walked past, so it was a random sample".
misconceptions.correction: Random means every member of the population has an equal (known) chance of selection, using a random process on a complete list. People who happen to walk past one place at one time do not give everyone that chance, so the sample is non-random and likely biased.

misconceptions.text: Thinks a larger sample removes bias, e.g. "the online poll had 20000 voluntary responses, so it must be representative".
misconceptions.correction: A larger sample reduces random variability, but it does not fix a biased method. Voluntary responders are people with strong opinions, however many there are. Fix the method (random selection) first; then increase the size for precision.
